paragraphs: Autumn came to Luoyang beneath a multitude of wagon ruts.

For three days and nights grain boats had been mooring on the canal, yet there was still no space at the wharves. Torches burned on either bank of the Luo River. Packhorses snorted in the mud left by the rain; junior clerks of the Ministry of War stood over wooden tablets crowded with figures, checking the names of the camps again and again. Fodder, armor, arrow feathers, medicines for the army surgeons—every item belonged somewhere, and every one might be exchanged or stolen. Even the coffin-maker had received an order. No report of battle deaths had arrived, but the men responsible for provisions had already asked whether he could set aside pinewood in case the army marched.
“Why prepare these before the fighting has even begun?” the carpenter asked.
“The generals are afraid there won’t be time,” said the runner.

Makeshift thatched shelters along the river were full of laborers drafted to move supplies. Old Zhou, a boatman of a Luoyang transport household, had brought grain ashore for the fifth time that year. A layer of skin had worn off his thumb, and the hemp cloth wrapped around it was sodden. His seventeen boats had to load and unload to the ministry’s timetable. Miss the opening of the downstream gates and the whole convoy would spend another night in the swift current. Patrols guarded the grain along both banks, yet the boatmen still feared leaks in the hulls. They slept with their ears against the planking and woke at the smallest trickle.

An old post station south of the city had been turned into a temporary infirmary. The camp had not yet marched, but drivers had broken legs in falls, carpenters had cut their hands shaping wood for siege crossbows, and porters working in the water day after day had contracted fever. The medical officer, unable to obtain enough bandages, took his camp pass to the expenditure office to argue. Its clerk pointed to the field hospital’s own accounts and refused to acknowledge a shipment of medicine chests that had not yet cleared the checkpoint. By dusk the wounded were still lying beside the road with nothing but a piece of oiled cloth over their heads.

An old man peered into the street through a crack in his door. In the torchlight a troop of Xianbei horsemen led their mounts past, wearing the same Qin insignia as the infantry from Guanzhong. Years ago he had watched Yan soldiers go down this very street, with different uniforms and different accents. Now every camp obeyed orders from Chang’an, though the hoofbeats on the paving stones sounded much as they had before.

On the eve of the review, the left army argued half the night over a consignment of new armor. The ordnance bureau insisted that the arrow-resistant cuirasses should go first to the advance guard on the waterways. A captain of Hedong infantry brought an arrow that had passed through an old breastplate during testing and led six of his men to the storehouse. The keeper dared not open the doors, but feared they would break the lock. When Fu Rong came, he did not ask which unit was entitled to collect first. He recorded the numbers of the six cracked suits of iron armor and ordered craftsmen to rivet them overnight. The next day there were a few irregular patches in the glittering ranks on the parade ground; not one soldier was made to stand in those six thin suits.

On the day of the review, armored men filled the southern bank of the Luo. Great banners lined the earthen slope, and the wind passing between them made a hillside of iron plates whisper. At the first beat of the drums the shield formations closed; at the second, the crossbows rose as one; at the third, cavalry threw up dust on both flanks. More than a hundred thousand men moved like the advancing tide, and a yellow haze slowly swallowed Luoyang’s southern gate. Fu Jian stood upon the high platform and watched for a long time.

He had seen armies all his life: the disorderly troops with whom he had contended for the throne against Fu Sheng, the elite cavalry that had swept away Former Yan, the expeditionary force carried by men and packhorses through the roads of Shu. Never before had soldiers of such different origins shown themselves willing to move at the beat of the same drum.

Beside him, Fu Pi recited the order of the formations. His voice was clear; he had plainly labored over it. Fu Jian listened, but his gaze settled on the rear of the marching host. Wagons, beasts of burden, and laborers carrying loads on shoulder poles stretched away in a gray line without an apparent end.
“A hundred and fifty thousand?” he asked.
“A hundred and fifty thousand fighting men. The contingents are still arriving. That does not include laborers or craftsmen.”
“And how many behind them?”
Fu Pi hesitated. “More than fifty thousand. More are joining all the way here.”
Fu Jian looked toward Fu Rong. His younger brother wore old armor and showed little pleasure in the spectacle.
“You are always complaining that my army lacks order. What do you think today?”
“It is in order.”
“Can it cross the Huai?”
“It can.”
“And the Yangtze?”
Fu Rong pointed behind the high platform, toward a dirt road cut into deep channels by wheels. “First ask how many roads running south from Luoyang can carry all these wagons.”
Fu Pi frowned. “Uncle always chooses the moment before battle to speak of difficulties.”
“Leave them unspoken, and men will die of them on the march.”
The drums rose again below the platform and drowned the silence between them.

That afternoon Fu Jian inspected the left camp himself. A Xianbei commandant knelt to present the military rolls. Fu Jian noticed that they now used the new company numbers assigned by the central military headquarters. The old marks for Yan units, Di units, and Han units were all gone. He asked whether the commandant had grown accustomed to the change. After a moment’s thought the man said, “A flag is quicker to recognize than an old lord. But when a unit scatters in the dark, the veterans still look first for men from their own villages.”
Fu Jian did not rebuke him. He told the commandant to rise and put the rolls away.

Entering the western camp, he found several laborers arguing beside a mule that had collapsed. Its hide had split beneath the lash, yet it would not get up. The officer in charge of the wagons said it needed only to go another thirty li before its load could be transferred. The laborers said it could not walk even one. Fu Jian ordered the baggage removed. He saw with his own eyes the bloody grooves pressed into the animal’s back. Grain sacks lay piled on the ground, and no one came at once to take charge of them.

The mule labored for breath for a long while and never rose again. Its driver unbuckled the bridle, got blood on his hands, and sat beside the road holding the worn harness. An attendant from the imperial camp said the loss could be entered in the accounts. But the driver kept asking whether his family would forfeit the two mu of wheat land pledged as surety now that the goods had not arrived. The military clerk pulled out the original service contract. It contained no provision for an animal dying on the road. Fu Jian ordered the contract sent to the expenditure office and forbade anyone to seize the pledged field in advance. Still the driver remained where he was until the grain sacks had been divided between two other wagons.
“Would it be the same north of the Huai?” Fu Jian asked.
The officer did not dare answer.
He ordered Fu Pi to investigate how many sick mules and overdue wagons there were in the camp. Fu Pi was displeased, but went to carry out the order.

At dusk charcoal fires were lit inside the command tent. Murong Chui unfolded a road map and pointed to a narrow stretch south of the Ru River. Water lay in the low fields on both sides. Tens of thousands of infantry could pass, but grain wagons would have to go one at a time. If the vanguard pressed ahead, the rear would inevitably fall apart. Fu Rong urged that the armies stop north of the Huai and send light cavalry to probe the defenses rather than crowding the whole host into the riverside flats.

Fu Pi laid a battle report before the emperor. “The Jin have repeatedly lost Xiangyang, and on the Huai they could not stand against our forces. If we do not advance today, must we wait until they have repaired their cities and raised more men, and let the chance slip away ourselves?”
“Have you ever seen a grain wagon keep pace with the men chasing a retreating enemy?” Murong Chui asked.
Fu Pi gave him a cold look. “The Champion General is always most skilled at explaining what other men cannot do.”

“I’m telling you what you can do this time. Send thirty thousand in the vanguard, with swift horses and sufficient provisions, to seize a favorable crossing. Keep the rest at Luoyang, and send grain forward every ten days. As long as the imperial camp remains here, a damaged road can still be repaired.”
“Then we lose our momentum,” Fu Pi said.
Murong Chui smiled faintly. “Momentum travels farthest. Grain travels slowest.”

Fu Jian told them to stop quarrelling. He had the military rolls and grain ledgers brought from headquarters and, after turning several pages, asked about a warehouse at Runan. The grain officer gave a figure two thousand hu short of yesterday’s report. Fu Jian ordered the two ledgers placed side by side. Sweat appeared on the officer’s forehead at once.

The clerk sent to inspect the stores first located the warehouse on the map, then checked the list of last night’s watchmen. The clay seal on the door was intact, yet two days earlier an order from the transport command had moved its grain sacks to a neighboring storehouse. The accounts still counted the same grain as stores in transit at Runan, allowing two camps to report full allotments. For the moment no one could calculate the true shortfall. Fu Pi wanted the storehouse clerk arrested; Fu Rong stopped him and ordered the officers of both stores to compare their ledgers and seals that night. The clerk breathed a little easier, then began to fear that both officers would arrive carrying falsified accounts.
“I am not asking how much you have embezzled,” Fu Jian said. “I am asking where that grain has gone.”
No one could answer.

After the ministers had withdrawn, Yao Chang emerged from behind the screen. He now held an office in charge of ritual and accompanied the emperor to oversee ceremonies, but the men around him still remembered the family histories of the commanders in every camp. He praised the day’s magnificent parade; Fu Jian listened without warmth. When Yao Chang spoke of which Qiang troops had grievances and which Hebei commandant longed for home, there was scarcely a detail he did not know.
“One would think you still commanded those troops,” Fu Jian said.
Yao Chang lowered his head. “When they meet an old acquaintance, they cannot help speaking of their troubles.”
“Let them speak to military headquarters. If they lack grain, I can supply it. If an order is wrong, I can change it. They need not go begging through you.”
Yao Chang bowed lower still. Outside the tent men were already urging the army onward, their footsteps following one another in file after file.

That night Fu Jian read a memorial sent from Chang’an by Crown Prince Fu Hong. Though suspended from his duties at the Secretariat, Hong had still written privately to his father about doubtful entries in the transport routes and reserve rolls. He did not urge the emperor to halt the advance southward. In one passage he wrote only that on the day the vanguard reached the northern bank of the Huai, they must also establish whether the roads back to Luoyang were open.
Fu Jian read the sentence twice and left the letter beneath the lamp.

The young attendant who tended the imperial lamp recognized Fu Hong’s handwriting. He had once copied marching schedules at the Secretariat. Seeing the emperor lay this particular sheet upon the campaign map, he ventured to ask whether the prince’s letter should be entered among the formal memorials after all. Fu Jian pondered, then said that a private letter could not serve as an edict moving troops, but its question had to be answered. Taking a clean sheet, he wrote to Fu Rong, ordering him to send road inspectors along the old Runan route and report that very night how many grain wagons the bridge could bear.

Close to midnight he stepped outside again. The lights of Luoyang were going out, but the camps shone to the horizon. An elderly Di soldier sat by the fire sewing his own boots, his stitches crooked and uneven. Fu Jian did not wake his guards. He only watched from a distance. Beside the old man lay a letter from home, its corner held down by a stone.

The following morning the central army issued its orders. Each contingent would move south in sequence, halt at appointed stages, and refrain from crossing the marked limits of its patrol zone. Fu Rong would oversee grain and supplies on the road back; Murong Chui would inspect the roads for the advance units; Fu Pi would lead the vanguard toward the northern bank of the Huai. The edict said nothing of crossing the Yangtze, nothing of destroying Jin with the strength of the entire realm. Every movement bore a deadline, a troop count, and a ration allotment, and every report had to be sent back to the Secretariat for verification.

Fu Jian mounted last. He turned to look at Luoyang. Along the Luo were still convoys unable to depart, and many laborers stood beside their wagons and knelt before the emperor. In the distance a storehouse clerk was leading a thin replacement mule through the mud.
He remembered something Wang Meng had said in his illness: a man need not finish in one lifetime all that he wishes to do.

Now, with the army before him, he still refused to admit that he might one day have to leave the realm to those who came after him. But when he heard a mule bray somewhere toward the end of the procession, he did not urge the red banner that signaled the army’s advance to move any faster.
The horns sounded at Luoyang’s southern gate.
